📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GTA 6 has been censored to a fairly large extent in Japan, where the country's strict ratings system often sees nudity, sexual content, and graphic violence be toned down or removed entirely in video games.

To be clear, GTA 6 has been given Japan's highest 18+ age rating — but it's still had to make changes in order to ensure its release in the region.

For starters, Rockstar's latest is packed with full-on nudity — to a degree never before seen in a mainstream release — but in Japan, it's apparently impossible to remove the underwear of main characters Jason and Lucia, even when they're taking a shower.

The same is true of NPCs — everyone's always wearing at least one layer to cover up their privates.

Sources indicate that needless to say, the game's numerous sex scenes have also been censored. Again, it's a case of keeping clothes on — but some specific scenes have actually been cut completely.

Violence is next on the list. GTA 6 obviously features a lot of bloodshed but it's also rather gory, with accurate depictions of dismemberment and lethal physical trauma. It can all come across as particularly gruesome given how realistic the game looks.

Sources indicate that in Japan, it seems as though most of this stuff is scaled back. There's less blood spray in general, and spilled blood doesn't stay in place very long.

It's a little unclear just how far this censorship of violence goes, but it's not uncommon for Japan to remove things like dismemberment — especially if a game's got a grounded setting.

In a recent development, for what it's worth, GTA 6 does have several settings that let you change the amount of blood and gore that's on display. I assume that in Japan, these settings are applied at a censored standard by default.

Interestingly, though, drug use seemingly hasn't been touched. Japan's got very strict anti-drug laws, but illegal goods are still totally usable in GTA 6.

Recent findings suggest that did you see this censorship coming? Try not to go on a blood-soaked rampage in the comments section below.

Each new GTA moves the series closer and closer to the original Mafia, the open-world game that bettered Rockstar

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that this week sees the release of Grand Theft Auto 6, the open-world crime 'em up that's been in development for at least eight years and has been waited on by fans for even longer.
  • Released less than a year after Grand Theft Auto 3, Mafia is perhaps a more prescient example of Rockstar's future than their own.
  • Set in Lost Heaven, a shoe-in for 1930s Chicago, Illinois, you play through Tommy Angelo's rise from a taxi driver, who has a chance run in with the Salieri crime family, to one of the gang's main enforcers in their fight against their rivals, the Morellos.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this week sees the release of Grand Theft Auto 6, the open-world crime 'em up that's been in development for at least eight years and has been waited on by fans for even longer. Naturally, over on PC we're still waiting for a port to be revealed, let alone a release date to circle in our calendars. But, as happens whenever a upcoming GTA is on the horizon, I think about Mafia: City of Lost Heaven.

Released less than a year after Grand Theft Auto 3, Mafia is perhaps a more prescient example of Rockstar's future than their own.

Set in Lost Heaven, a shoe-in for 1930s Chicago, Illinois, you play through Tommy Angelo's rise from a taxi driver, who has a chance run in with the Salieri crime family, to one of the gang's main enforcers in their fight against their rivals, the Morellos.

The influences on developers Illusion Softworks are obviously cinematic, with whole sequences ripped from The Godfather films and Goodfellas (and I'd argue there's a sprinkling of Once Upon A Time In America for good measure). A habit they share with Rockstar, who also pull liberally from crime films that share the settings of their games. But Illusion Softworks are also clearly interested in capturing the history of the Prohibition era, too. The story begins in the aftermath of the 1929 Wall Street Crash and the depression that followed, running through until the late 30s, and you see that time pass in the city around you. Buildings that are under construction at the start of the game are completed by its end, a used car lot in Chinatown sits empty for most of the game until business picks up with the economy, but most enjoyable of all is that the cars driving the streets change. At first the roads are filled with Ford Model-T-inspired vehicles that basically look like horse carriages with engines, but by the end of the game they've all become much sleeker creatures that have left their early carriage influences behind.

The city Illusion Softworks built also has a dedication to verisimilitude that we see Rockstar adopting in their later games. As you drive Lost Heaven's streets, you must pay attention to speed limits and red lights, as speeding and running traffic lights will both earn you a fine if a policeman spots you. For fans of public transport, there are streetcars and overhead trams you can ride to navigate the city, too. Two other touches I love: when you reload your gun, you dump the whole clip instead of returning the unfired bullets to a magic ammo reservoir, and vehicles can run out of fuel if you drive them too far.

In a recent development, much had been made of all the simulations running under the surface of Grand Theft Auto 6, such as fully realised cloud formation, a smell reaction system, and… fuel tanks that can run empty. No doubt they're significantly more impressive than what's on show in Mafia, and this isn't about putting the two games against each other (even if one of them was likely made for less than the other studio spent on coffee runs across its eight-year development). Nor is it about saying history recognised the wrong game: Grand Theft Auto 3 was a huge step forward in open-world gaming and Mafia was recognised and celebrated in its time. It's about something else.

Sources indicate that back in 2002, Illusion Softworks offered a different kind of open-world crime game. One that was more mature despite having a lower age rating. Grand Theft Auto was undoubtedly more influential, sparking imitators that mostly opted to follow its tone and sensibilities – Saints Row began in a similar place to GTA 3 and as the series continued leaned further into the silliness and parody, for instance. But while for many years Mafia stood as a sign to an open world path that could have been taken, the longer Grand Theft Auto series has gone on, the more Rockstar have found their way toward the example set by Illusion Softworks. The games are still aiming for bombastic comedy at times, but they're also interested in the likes of newly-arrived-in-America Niko Belic, or Michael de Santa, a retired criminal haunted by his past. They're much richer protagonists than Claude, the silent character you play in GTA 3.

In a recent development, the Mafia series has continued, marked by ideas that remain as interesting as what was on show in the original. In Mafia 3, you play Lincoln Clay, a black soldier returned from the war in Vietnam and brought into the family. Set in a take on New Orleans, Louisiana, during the civil rights movement, you face overt racism. Linger too long in white, wealthy neighbourhoods and the residents will call on the police to move you along. And the Definitive Edition remake of the first game, released in 2020, is a rare example of a game that both captures the spirit of the original and justifies its existence by expanding and bettering the story. Though I don't think any of its sequels have been as innovative, nor as forward thinking, as the first game.

I don't want to come across as Rockstar-bashing. The studio have continued to push the open-world genre forward with every release and I want to see what other developers lift from GTA 6 for their own games. But I'm even more pleased that as the studio's aged, their work has grown closer to Illusion Softworks'.

PlayStation defeats £2 billion UK lawsuit that alleged Sony forced consumers into "excessive and unfair prices"

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (478 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sony has defeated a major £2 billion UK class action lawsuit concerning the price of games on the PlayStation Store (thanks, TheGameBusiness).
  • Sources indicate that the case, brought by Alex Neill, who said she represented roughly 12.2 million gamers, accused Sony of applying "excessive and unfair" pricing on games that appeared on the storefront accessible by PS3, PS4 and PS5 consoles - the PlayStation Store.
  • "Potential PlayStation console purchasers had both access to sufficient information and an incentive to consider that information in order to make informed purchasing decisions at the console level, especially in the case of high-value consumers who spend significant amounts in the digital gaming aftermarket," read the judgment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sony has defeated a major £2 billion UK class action lawsuit concerning the price of games on the PlayStation Store (thanks, TheGameBusiness). The judgment came after a 30-day Competition Appeal Tribunal that took place in London, where PlayStation users claimed Sony had removed "all actual and potential competition" in relation to selling digital games on the console.

Sources indicate that the case, brought by Alex Neill, who said she represented roughly 12.2 million gamers, accused Sony of applying "excessive and unfair" pricing on games that appeared on the storefront accessible by PS3, PS4 and PS5 consoles - the PlayStation Store. In a judgment published by the London’s Competition Appeal Tribunal today (17th November), the case was rejected. The judgement noted that market definitions used to define Sony's conduct were "unsafe", and that consumers "would be likely to make informed choices when purchasing consoles" and games on the hardware, too.

"Potential PlayStation console purchasers had both access to sufficient information and an incentive to consider that information in order to make informed purchasing decisions at the console level, especially in the case of high-value consumers who spend significant amounts in the digital gaming aftermarket," read the judgment.

Industry observers note that the lawsuit made the argument that, upon purchasing a PS5 or other PlayStation console, you were then trapped within its ecosystem, and forced into paying the prices determined by Sony. The Tribunal disagreed, however, and ruled that Sony competed within a wider 'systems market' alongside Xbox, Nintendo and PC, for example. Furthermore, the Tribunal found no evidence that the existence of other digital storefronts would have actually brought any PlayStation Store pricing down.

Interestingly, the Tribunal used the argument that consumers can also opt and buy physical games instead of using the PlayStation Store - something that is changing as of the start of 2028. That did not seem to have any bearing on today's decision, though. It's also worth noting that this case did not seek to interrogate the ownership status of digital games - something that's been at the heart of the movement rallying against Sony's decision to kill off physical media. Earlier this year, spokespeople from Sony's legal team argued "reasonable consumers" already know they don't actually own their digital games.

The London Tribunal has a fairly long history. Back in 2022, it began as a case that attempted to sue Sony to the tune of £5bn for "ripping people off" on PlayStation Store. Sony argued the case brought against it in this trial was "flawed from start to finish". This isn't the only situation where we're seeing consumers pursue legal action against the platform holder. Last year, PlayStation was sued in the Netherlands over the so-called "Sony tax" that highlighted artificially inflated prices on the Store, and sought to represent more than 20,000 participants that felt short-changed by the organization.

Five Things I Wish I'd Known Before Getting a Foldable Phone

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1337 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The iPhone Duo might be the highest profile foldable phone to date, but it’s by no means the first.
  • One of the most notable aspects of the iPhone Duo is how wide its screen is, even while closed.
  • Compare with my Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which features an extremely tall 2.17:1 aspect ratio when closed, but a nearly square 1:04:1 aspect ratio when open.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The iPhone Duo might be the highest profile foldable phone to date, but it’s by no means the first. Personally, I’ve had my eye on the Google variant, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold—and recently I finally took the plunge. I thought I’d done my research to know how different having a foldable phone would be, but I still had a bit to learn. Here are some of the things I wish I’ve learned along the way after making the jump to foldables.

One of the most notable aspects of the iPhone Duo is how wide its screen is, even while closed. And there’s a good reason for that: The larger screen while open has exactly the same 1.41:1 aspect ratio as the smaller screen while closed. This has a ripple effect on how every app you use looks and feels—and whether you like Apple’s approach is largely a matter of personal preference.

Compare with my Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which features an extremely tall 2.17:1 aspect ratio when closed, but a nearly square 1:04:1 aspect ratio when open. On the outer screen, apps are a little less wide than on my old phone, but there’s plenty of space for reading books or articles on the inner screen.

Sources indicate that I like the tall, thin display personally because it feels easier to reach buttons with my thumb, and the wider display is better for reading. However, this approach can occasionally result in some odd app layouts. Not every app is designed for tablets, especially on Android, and shifting the aspect ratio between the inner and outer display sometimes means re-rendering or even restarting an app entirely to load properly.

The iPhone Duo has a more consistent aspect ratio and general feel between the inner and outer display, but it comes at the cost of a really wide phone. Neither approach is better or worse on its own, but it might be worth going to a local store to get your hands on the phone you’re thinking about before buying.

For years, the screens on most smartphones have been made of increasingly tough and scratch-resistant glass. So tough that you might not even need a screen protector anymore. On a foldable phone, that can be true of the outside display, but it’s very much not when it comes to the inner, foldable display.

Screens might be foldable, but the strong, durable glass that makes your phone so scratch-resistant isn’t. No matter what foldable phone you use, the covering on the inner display will be more flexible, and thus softer. Apple uses a nano-texture polymer film that can be replaced, but the film on most foldable phones cannot. That means if they get damaged or scratched, those marks will be there for the life of your phone.

Industry observers note that if you (like me) haven’t considered a screen protector in a while, it might be time to try one again, at least for the inner display. It’s also worth keeping in mind how rough you blueprint to be with your phone. Construction sites or factories might not be the best home for a foldable phone you plan to open a lot, but an office job should be a bit safer.

It has been revealed that similar to the screen protector glitch, cases can be more of a headache. Most rigid cases will come in two pieces, and the piece that covers the outer display can be shockingly minimal—barely more than a frame, for some of the cases I looked at. A poorly made case can be brittle or pop off more easily, so it’s more notable to get a high-quality one.

If you like to use your phone case as your wallet, it’s also notable to be wary of cases that aren’t specifically designed for your model of phone (and maybe some that are). A lot of wallet cases are built to unfold to reveal your phone’s screen on one side, and your cards and ID on the other. But depending on how your foldable phone unfolds, it could be awkward to reach the inner screen.

According to recent reports, the hinge also introduces more spaces for dust and debris to get into your phone. Despite the extra moving parts and gaps, most foldable phones still offer the now-standard IP68 dust and water resistance rating. That mainly applies to what can get inside and damage the components inside your phone. It’s still possible for hair and dirt to get gummed up in any pinchable spaces, so look out for any case that might provide even more nooks for dust to collect in.

It has been revealed that I’ve set up most of my apps how I like them by now, but when I first got my foldable phone, I had to revisit some settings I thought I was done messing with. One of the most notable examples was my ebook apps: I was previously using a single-column, medium-font layout, but it looked ridiculous on the inner display. After switching to a two-column layout, it not only felt more natural, but a lot like reading a regular book.

Sources indicate that similarly, there were some uses for my calendar app that got a whole lot more useful. I’ve never really been able to use anything other than either the one-day or Schedule view if I want to make out anything, but on the inner screen, I can finally look at my week at a glance. But that meant tweaking some things—like showing reminders, which fit naturally amid my events in Schedule view, but become a cluttered mess when I saw 14 different reminders to take my meds at once in the Week view.

Most apps do a decent job of automatically adjusting to different screen sizes, but I found a few outliers that I had to figure out myself. As an example, Google Docs would default to a view with extremely tiny text when I first started using it. It took me a bit to figure out that this was due to a “Print layout” toggle in the document’s settings. This is, for some reason, enabled by default when opening a document on the larger inner screen. It can take some time to learn the eccentricities of all your apps, but it’s worth poking around when you can.

I know, it sounds so obvious, right? The outer screen is the one you’ll use most often, so how could you forget about it? But when you unfold the inner screen, the outer one is still useful in some surprising ways that I hadn’t even considered until I went poking around in some of my apps.

It has been revealed that one of the most adorable examples is the Made You Look feature in the Pixel’s Camera app. When unfolded, you can take a picture using the rear camera and see a preview like normal, while the outer screen reveals silly animations to capture the attention of a baby or toddler that you want to look into the camera. Admittedly, this is an older feature, but it’s a clever one. For adults, you can also use the outer display to get a selfie preview while using the rear-facing camera.

Sources indicate that the outer screen is also just better for some things. YouTube is one of the few apps that has a unique layout designed for a partially folded screen, with the video playing on the tilted-up portion of the screen, and video controls on the bottom portion.

However, in my experience, it was a lot nicer to watch a YouTube video by just propping up the outer screen by unfolding the phone a bit, like a kickstand. My Pixel even detected when YouTube was in full-screen mode on the outer display and would be more forgiving of unfolding the phone without switching to the inner screen. The phone anticipated I might just want to prop up the smaller screen, which I thought was a nice touch.

Industry observers note that as highlighted by Sakurai on social media, the Switch 2 exclusive is officially one year old as of this week. It's received multiple updates since launch and Nintendo recently rolled out the last two amiibo.

In the game director's message, he also touches on his future as a game creator. Here's a rough translation of this part of Sakurai's post via EventHubs: "Time flies. I wonder how much more I'll be able to make".

If we do hear any significant updates about Sakurai's future projects, or anything else he is up to, we'll be sure to let you know.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Knowing how to get a jet in GTA 6 is essential information if you're planning to cause chaos, as taking control of one of these military aircraft is considered peak criminal behavior. While you'd expect that significant progress in GTA 6 would be required before you even had a chance of swiping such high-end hardware, you can actually go and help yourself to one pretty much as soon as you start the game. To try it yourself, here's how to steal a jet in GTA 6.

The location for a number of GTA 6 jets is the Mile Zero Air Station, which is found by heading west along the main road from the starting area, through Abismo Key, then on to Southwind and the military base itself.

You can drive there in any vehicle, though I recommend not using your GTA 6 personal vehicle as it will get trashed and left inside the base, so steal a sturdy and reasonably fast vehicle for the job. Purchasing and equipping body armor from Ammu-nation will also improve your odds of surviving the initial stage.

Follow the route marked on my map above, which will lead you through some barriers on the road to a set of soldiers who will open fire, then take the first turning right and drive through more soldiers until you see a dirt pile ahead that you can hit to clear the security fences. This is also a Stunt Jump, though you don't need to complete it as long as you clear the perimeter and land on the runway.

Once on the runway inside the miliary base, drive straight ahead to where you'll see several GTA 6 jets parked up next to hangars. Pull up alongside one, jump out of your car and hop straight into the cockpit, before firing up the afterburner and turning onto the runway to take off. If you'd prefer to swipe a GTA 6 tank instead, turn left when you land on the runway and look to the left hand side of the large building.

It has been revealed that once you've taken control of your jet and got airborne, follow the prompt to retract the landing gear and you're away! Be aware that you'll have attracted at least a five-star GTA 6 Wanted Level with this theft, which could go up to six if you start blowing things up, so multiple military jets will be scrambled to shoot you down with homing missiles. I was barely able to reach the first bridge before getting blown out of the sky, but if you fly low and take evasive action you may fare better – good luck!

If you're looking for an impressive ride that's easier to obtain then here's how to steal the GTA 6 Paul Walker car, which you can then use to arrive in style at the various GTA 6 Strip Club locations around Leonida.

#131948. My murderous wine merchant whines for a chance at republican rule in Crusader Kings 3’s Silk and Silver expansion, which isn't only about the money

My murderous wine merchant whines for a chance at republican rule in Crusader Kings 3’s Silk and Silver expansion, which isn't only about the money

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2088 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The tentacles of my trade empire snake up towards France in the west, down towards Africa in the south, and off into Hungary in the east.
  • In a recent development, I’ve shed blood in its name, the blood of someone else named Marco no less.
  • It should, in theory, help that he’s my best mate, thanks to a well-timed feast.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The tentacles of my trade empire snake up towards France in the west, down towards Africa in the south, and off into Hungary in the east. Yet, I still can’t reach out and grasp the throne that sits right in front of me. I’m Marco Sanudo, and the throne of the serene republic of Venice eludes me.

In a recent development, I’ve shed blood in its name, the blood of someone else named Marco no less. I’ve managed to avoid punishment for that crime, despite the fact it earned me a fiefdom to rule while I’ve tried to up my patrician score enough to be the lucky party the next time a ruling Doge dies in office (or runs out their 10 year term). Sadly, Doge Leonardo, the mysterious masked lord who’s had an iron grip on power since the first couple of old blokes to hold the position in this playthrough popped their clogs, is proving incredibly tough to oust.

It should, in theory, help that he’s my best mate, thanks to a well-timed feast. It certainly did in being granted a pardon for offing that other Marco, but not even that and a plague which infected nearly everyone in the realm aside from me have paved the way to Dogedom. In the meantime, I’ve striven to gain wealth and influence. I’ve worked up to having four trade routes running at once, with goods like wine, iron, and textiles flowing from market to market across southern Europe and bringing a steady supply of coin back to my Venetian estate. I’ve built trade posts at the extremities of my routes, giving me the option of starting from further afield and reaching latest lands if the cash flow dries up closer to home.

This is where Crusader Kings 3’s Silk and Silver expansion has blended a bit with the game’s traditional feudal moneymaking to supercharge my coffers. The land holding I killed a dude for, the Proveditorate of Zara, means I’ve also had tax money from modern day Croatia to add to both my trade profits and the income my domicile generates on its own. I am, as the medieval kids say, minted.

Recent findings suggest that getting to the point of serious pocket clinkage is, as you might imagine given Silk and Silver’s focus on filling the game’s world with travelling merchant companies and wheeler-dealing republican patrician families, the beating heart of the expansion. A near-constant stream of notifications about prices of different goods I’m trying to hawk in different locations encourage me to regularly prune and re-work my routes so that max profits are being earned and no carrying capacity’s being wasted. The bubbling up of wars and plagues impacts prices in affected cities, making it a never-ending battle if you’re desperate to optimise everything within an inch of its life. I’ve found that degree of micromanagement unnecessary if the goal is just to keep a decent profit margin ticking over. Just remember to replace the trader assigned to a route if they die, recall them every few years so they don’t stress themselves to death, and check in every so often to re-evaluate whether you’re running goods that are suitably in demand.

Sources indicate that if you stick at it for a decent amount of time, with a certain type of good - alcohol or jewellery, for example - your expertise in dealing in them increases, making it easier to sell for better prices. Trade routes left running between the same markets also gain boons from being in place for a long time, offering a counterpoint to rejigging them every five seconds to wring out a few more coins. Most of my routes have run along a path that includes stops at four markets, with the occasional location boasting a monopoly I’ve bargained for with the local ruler, so I don’t have to worry about competition at every stop.

Recent findings suggest that when you’re playing as a merchant who isn’t locked into the ruling inner circle of a republic, making your routes as lengthy as possible is one of the three moneymaking areas your company can specialise in. That first one’s caravaneering, and is the one I leant into in a non-Marco Sanudo playthrough. Beyond that, you can become an expert loan shark, lending cash to rulers or paying their ransoms in order to recoup interest and collect hooks you can use for favours. Manufacturing expensive artifacts that can be sold individually to collectors for a profit is the third option. The latter two I’ve only dabbled in a little bit as of writing, having earned enough gold mostly from caravanneering to buy the land containing the city with my home market and be anointed a Sheikh. So, beginning as a landless merchant is a nice alternative to Crusader Kings 3’s long-established wandering adventurer starting point, with both allowing you to work your way up from lowly serf to landed lordly dynasty in your location of choice.

According to recent reports, if you’re after a more specific historical scenario, Silk and Silver has Guelphs and Ghibellines. This is where we find Marco Sanudo, as well as the other patrician family head I’ve played as thus far, Speronella Dalesmanni. The setup is that the Pope and the Holy Roman Emperor have had a bit of a tiff, essentially rooted in who should have certain powers, with different cities and powerful families in northern Italy taking either the Guelph (Pope-likers) or Ghibelline (Holy Roman Empire-enjoyers) side depending on what suits their goals or principles. I’ll be honest, aside from being another way to easily earn friends or enemies in the ruthless crucible of merchant republican politics, where votes and reputation-bolstering aid from other nobles are key, the situation’s not had a hugely obvious bearing on my playthroughs thus far.

I think the closest it’s come is during my Dalesmanni run, if largely due to the existence of the By God Alone expansion allowing a upcoming branch of Catholicism, dubbed Italian Christianity, to be created. The initial conversion push from the bishop responsible led a number of my fellow northern Italian nobles away from the Roman Rite headed by his Popeliness, making the Guelph/Ghibelline split more clearly defined.

According to recent reports, in the early hours of both my Sanudo and Dalesmanni playthroughs, I’ve been far more focused on simply trying to push the respective patrician families up the hill from posh toffs with naught but a vote and a manor to elected rulers of their great cities, with land holdings to match. Speronella’s situation in Padua is made incredibly tough by the fact she’s a woman in a world where every succession rule is designed to put blokes first, so I’ve had more success with Marco and his quest to become the Doge of Venice.

Sources indicate that as the head of a patrician family, one of select few elite clans who steer the oligarchical republic, I was faced with earning Marco enough respect among his fellow family heads that they’d consider voting him to the top of the succession list, thus securing his power whenever the current Doge got the boot. Pulling that off, while also not kowtowing to the requests and schemes of those same peers, isn’t easy. A large cocktail of factors go into determining whether another noble likes you enough to vote in support of your succession. There’s your patrician rating, which is upped by doing things which specifically show you to be good at this Italian noble house lark, such as establishing trade monopolies for the republic, gaining the Pope’s favour, or having close relatives who also hold key positions in the republic. However, how close a friendship you have with the target and how their character traits align with you also play a huge rule.

Thus it was that, at one point, Marco was best mates with the current Doge and had a decent patrician rating, but had only amassed 68 of the 72 points needed for said Doge to vote for him because the Doge was generous, and therefore didn’t care for Marco’s ambitiousness. That same Doge either liked or respected Marco enough to grant him a council position and the status of regent, but he would not back Marco to replace him permanently for love nor money. This is the same man who liked Marco so much that when I pulled off that not-so-sneaky murder on another noble house head in order to inherit the keys to the Proveditorate of Zara, the Doge was instantly willing to pardon me and prevent Marco suffering any punishment for the crime.

It has been revealed that not even a couple of serious plagues hitting Venice, which at one point had all three people ahead of Marco in the queue suffering from smallpox, could get him on that throne. Eventually, it took a bit of lucky timing when his Doge mate died of old age - a few years after beating smallpox - to finally install Marco as Doge. Given that delayed promotion, as of writing I’ve not yet had enough time in the substantial chair to give a proper verdict on how it differs from regular feudal rulerdom in the long run.

What I can do instead is tell you a bit about the fun of council votes. The same pool of voters who in a republic like Venice, get a say in who succeeds the ruler, also vote on the passage of laws and decrees. One proposal you can put forward is a vote to change who exactly is allowed a seat in this voting pool. It defaults to just being heads of patrician families, but can be extended to include all vassals, or tightened up so only the Doge’s councillors or the ruler themselves have a say, that being the way despotism lies. As you can imagine, passing a change to who can vote can drastically change the state of play, either tightening up the number of folks who might oppose or support you, or bringing latest folks into play in a fashion that dilutes individual power, but gives you more pieces on the board to mind or manipulate to your advantage.

I’ve found it suitably tough to orchestrate successful votes to change laws and customs which medieval Italian noble families, expectedly, have firmly entrenched stances on. Getting rid of checks and balances, such as the requirement to vote on banishments or wars - so the Doge can rule as a despot - has proven one such challenge, as has changing laws governing men being prioritised over women. I tried to pass equal succession as a substitute for men being put first while playing as Speronella, but met an insurmountable wall of resistance due to the region’s culture and faith. So, all I could do was try to put my young male heir in the best position possible to make the sorts of gains I couldn’t.

It has been revealed that much easier to weasel into place, either through some canny swaying or the offering of hooks, are laws giving state backing or other priority to trading in certain types of goods. Alcohol, for instance, which certainly hasn’t hurt the profits of Marco’s two wine trade routes.

It has been revealed that thus, cash continues to flow through the tentacles of my trade empire in sizable globs. As he’s now Doge, I’ve got Marco using the ample funds of Venice’s treasury to build a newly introduced piazza and have him focused on making the city’s already-strong trade league even more formidable, by attracting new members from the few other northern Italian blocs.

While I’m fairly sure there are folks who’ll find Silk and Silver's constant barrage of trade route notifications annoying, or that their power-grabbing skills and sheer multitude of money-making means combine to make playthroughs less challenging than they could be, so far I've found it another enjoyably sonorous string to Crusader Kings 3’s bow. Above all else, playing as a merchant gives more reason to invest in stewardship skills beyond just maximising your tax yields, while the republican politics of the DLC's main region fleshes out rewarding intrigue-focused builds. Diplomacy and martial skills are less key, but still have their place at times.

If you’re an absolute stickler for historical accuracy, you may well find other things to gripe about, but aside from the Guelph and Ghibelline conflict fading into the background, I’ve found plenty to like in my quest to become top Doge.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the Sims 4 players on PlayStation and Xbox have now caught up to their friends on PC, at least when it comes to the game’s Marketplace.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the Sims 4 players on PlayStation and Xbox have now caught up to their friends on PC, at least when it comes to the game’s Marketplace. This new feature is essentially a hub for paid mods and other user-created content.

As often happens when long-established games introduce paid mods, The Sims 4’s wasn’t especially well-received, in part because of the introduction of a newly introduced premium currency - Moola - that is the only way to purchase any of that content.

The Moola denominations and prices are similar to many other in-game currencies, and the criticism around them is the same: they obfuscate the true value of items, and because of the way those denominations are structured, you’ll never be able to buy exactly what you need.

For most games, the subject of paid mods has always been fraught, and that's certainly true for The Sims 4. In the announcement blog post, Maxis said that the launch on consoles will work similarly to what PC players have seen, in that Kits will no longer be available to buy directly with real money on the PlayStation and Microsoft Stores. While Expansion Packs, Game Packs, and Stuff Packs will remain, you’ll need to buy Moola if you want to acquire Kits going forward.

In a recent development, interestingly, however, EA seems to have changed its mind somewhat on the Kits situation. A recently leaked memo (via SimsCommunity), appears to show that the publisher intends on making Kits available for purchase directly again, without the need for Moola.

Unfortunately, this only appears to affect the PC version, with the reversion reportedly forthcoming on both the EA App as well as Steam. Indeed, according to the same report, the change has already taken place on the former, with the latter following on April 20.

Considering the Marketplace only just launched on consoles, the firm may wait to see if the decision to remove Kits from console platform marketplaces will be as poorly received as it has been on PC.

If you’re looking to jump back into The Sims 4 to check out all the new paid content, make sure you’re well-equipped with our list of Sims 4 cheats and debug options, or this one specifically for the Royalty & Legacy expansion cheats.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • With GTA 6, Rockstar has created a game few other developers could even dream of competing with.
  • In a recent development, 21% of Rockstar, representing about 1,000 employees, have been at the organization for more than 10 years, a spokesperson tells Bloomberg.
  • According to recent reports, nintendo offers one of the most notable counter-examples, where the same five developers who worked on the original Super Mario Bros.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With GTA 6, Rockstar has created a game few other developers could even dream of competing with. That's partly down to the game's lengthy development cycle and massive budget, but you can also thank Rockstar's willingness to keep its veteran employees around when so many other studios are willing to lay off their most experienced developers.

In a recent development, 21% of Rockstar, representing about 1,000 employees, have been at the organization for more than 10 years, a spokesperson tells Bloomberg. Admittedly, that tenure only covers two major new releases – Red Dead Redemption 2 and GTA 6 – but developers with a decade or more of experience at a single studio are becoming a rare breed.

According to recent reports, nintendo offers one of the most notable counter-examples, where the same five developers who worked on the original Super Mario Bros. were still in the credits of Super Mario Bros. Wonder nearly 40 years later. Rockstar hasn't been around for 40 years, but many of the names you'll find in the credits have been there since the PS2 era, when GTA fever had just started to reach its absurd highs.

Other publishers, meanwhile, are laying off even their most experienced staff by the bucketload. Devs like Fallout's Tim Cain are warning of the consequences of cutting off institutional knowledge even as Microsoft cuts off developers who'd been making megahits like The Elder Scrolls for decades. How can The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel live up to expectations when the people who know how to make Elder Scrolls games are constantly being laid off?

Clearly, Rockstar has been more willing to hang onto its veteran staff – unless, of course, we're talking about the 34 union-associated employees it fired in 2025. Disputes over those firings and the union itself are still ongoing, and ugly allegations about continued crunch at Rockstar are coming up as a result.

In a recent development, on top of all that, GTA 6 devs are "worried about getting laid off" even after "working on the biggest game of all time," and it's clear that there's no true insulation from the threat of layoffs when an executive decides your name is on the wrong side of a spreadsheet. Those fears remain even as GTA 6 itself stands as a monolithic example of what a group of experienced developers are truly capable of.

Grand Theft Auto 6 success isn't enough to stop the layoffs, former Square Enix exec argues, as Rockstar has "built the biggest, most expensive game of all time and now released it".

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more.

He's been covering games (with occasional dalliances in the worlds of anime and pro wrestling) since 2015, first as a freelancer, then as a news writer at PCGamesN for nearly five years. His love for games was sparked somewhere between Metal Gear Solid 2 and Knights of the Old Republic, and these days you can usually find him splitting his entertainment time between retro gaming, the latest big action-adventure title, or a long haul in American Truck Simulator.

Now it’s being played by millions, actress Lexie Shoaibi has revealed she stars as the character, who not-so subtly throws herself at Jason during a very early story mission.

I actually think this is one example of the game’s slightly more mature writing. Wait, don’t roll your eyes – just hear me out, okay?

One post by Complex, featuring a few images and the caption ‘Mandy from GTA 6’, attracted 37 million views in just a few hours. Pertinently, it’s been bookmarked 54k times.

I don’t want to analyse this character too deeply, but I think it’s the moment I realised Rockstar has really pushed the boat out here.

Industry observers note that the sheer variety of body types, and the detail invested into them, is unprecedented really. Mandy is just one of many similarly realistic NPCs in the game.

And while the character is almost certainly a psychopath, it’s been amusing to see her go viral overnight.

Enjoy all the upcoming followers, Lexie!

Spirit Crossing, the new Zelda-ish hangout MMO from the creators of Cozy Grove, understands that sometimes you just want to be alone

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that new multiplayer game Spirit Crossing offers up a visually blissful, but inwardly draconian world in which other people are not allowed to talk to you – indeed, not permitted access to the visible electromagnetic spectrum – unless you have given them a high five.
  • Deign to slap somebody's hand, and they'll pop into colour and be able to join you for various activities.
  • According to recent reports, there's nothing forcing you to do any of this in company, mind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that new multiplayer game Spirit Crossing offers up a visually blissful, but inwardly draconian world in which other people are not allowed to talk to you – indeed, not permitted access to the visible electromagnetic spectrum – unless you have given them a high five. By default, players appear to each other as shadows, all exploring a skybound landscape of magic animals and layer-cake mountains that reminds me of both Sable and The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom.

Deign to slap somebody's hand, and they'll pop into colour and be able to join you for various activities. For example, going fishing, playing instruments round the campfire, playing dress-up and pulling emotes in group photos, bouncing around on strangely inflated yaks, or questing forth to heal troubled spirits. There's some material gathering and crafting, and there are recurring storms that make the ambience more threatening, but overcoming a challenge doesn't feel like the point of Spirit Crossing. The "missions" are just an excuse to hang out together.

According to recent reports, there's nothing forcing you to do any of this in company, mind. "Stay a mysterious shadow, lend a hand when you feel like it, and disappear before anyone can make it weird," the devs explain, adding a hug emoji to make plain that they don't think you're some kind of smelly misanthrope for shunning other players.

I, personally, am a smelly misanthrope, and will only ever appear in your game as a skulking opacity, peering through the window of your personal gingerbread house, with its tastefully accessorised lava lamps and throw rugs. No, I will not join you for a group hang-glider tour. No, I do not want to play the banjo with you. You will experience me only as the nagging sensation of being watched, while you chat to the local "Stylesmith" about fetching rucksack patterns.

Spirit Crossing has an upfront cost that "gives players full access to the complete game experience in perpetuity", but you can also take out a subscription for some cosmetic items and access to a "limited resource exchange shop". They're avoiding traditional microtransactions, which is nice.

According to recent reports, spry Fox are also the developers of Cozy Grove - "the best grove since Byker", wrote Graham, in one of his regular 'senior moments'. I myself know them as the studio behind wintry puzzler Road Not Taken, with its randomised woodlands, and block-merging city builder Triple Town, with its unexpectedly terrifying bears. Little about Spirit Crossing seems terrifying, unless you count the shadow loitering at the edge of your conversation pit.

According to recent reports, you can read more about the game on Steam. I find Spirit Crossing quite novel, especially when it dispenses with the WholeCosy "discover your inner fashonista" stuff and leans into the supernatural elements: I like the idea of hunkering by the campfire during a storm, watching the clouds hurtle past. Still, I'm disappointed to hear that Spry Fox have made use of generative AI during its creation.

Sources indicate that as has been pointed out to us on Bluesky, the developers called on Anthropic's Claude tools for various behind-the-scenes tasks - the example they give in a Discord post is editing several config files at once. There's no disclosure on the game's Steam page because Spry Fox haven't used AI tools to generate any of the art or music - Valve rewrote Steam's disclosure requirements in January to exempt the usage of generative AI for "efficiency gains", which the above presumably falls under.

It's hardly a full-throated endorsement of generative AI, but it still forms part of a political and cultural project I consider reckless and morbid. For a longer account of my objections, albeit one that doesn't cover Claude in particular, here's my longform thinkywangle from July last year.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It took Battlefield Studios over four months to tell Battlefield 6 players what they can actually expect from the game over the course of this year, in terms of content - but we’re glad to see a blueprint laid out nonetheless.

The developer unveiled a grand 2026 roadmap, covering three more seasons right now in the works, and a wealth of new additions across the entire game, including new maps and the introduction of a new theatre of combat.

In a wide-ranging fresh video dubbed The Year Ahead, members of the Battlefield 6 development team have revealed a lot of new information about the future of the multiplayer shooter, going over plenty of the features and new content coming over the course of this year.

In a recent development, the video confirmed that BF6 has at least three other seasons in the works. Season 3, which begins in May, will be followed by Season 4, and Season 5 later in the year. Season 5 is the most mysterious, which is understandable.

We’ve known about some of what’s coming in Season 3, such as the remake of Golmud Railway (now called Railway to Golmud), but the video also revealed that a remake of Battlefield 3’s Grand Bazaar - now Cairo Bazaar - will also arrive later in the same season. Other exciting additions, such as battle royale solos and ranked play for Redsec are also on the agenda for Season 3.

In a recent development, season 4, set for July, looks to be the biggest so far, with the introduction of naval combat, which will be available across two maps. Tsuru Reef, which is said to be even larger than Golmud, the largest map in BF6. The Pacific-set map won’t be the only one, as later in the season, another remake will arrive, this time of the iconic Wake Island.

Industry observers note that the introduction of naval combat will bring with it a fresh dynamic wave system, aircraft carriers with operational flight decks, and new naval vehicles. Custom lobbies and Spectator Mode are also planned for Season 4.

Season 5 will bring three maps to BF6, rather than two, but all of its content remains under wraps.

According to recent reports, perhaps a sour note is that almost all of the maps referenced and shown in the video are remakes of maps from other Battlefield games, or reimagined at the very least. The Battlefield series is no stranger to remaking its own maps, but Battlefield 6 appears to be leaning on it much more than past entries.

If it’s any consolation, however, the map remakes we’ve played so far in Battlefield 6 have gone through major changes that have contributed to giving them a different flow and feel from their classic versions, or even remakes in other BF games.

Over the course of 2026, you can also expect the return of persistent servers, as well as a server browser to find them all - just like the good ol’ days. This includes the ability to host your own, though it’s unclear quite how this is going to work.

Season 3 is set to revealed in the coming days, so you’ll be hearing back from BF Studios in the near future.

Take-Two Interactive, the parent company of Rockstar Games, has published GTA 6's day-one retail sales, and they're predictably astronomical and record-breaking.

Via BusinessWire, Rockstar and Take-Two announce that GTA 6's launch day sales, based on estimates through end of day on November 19, reached $3.79 billion, surpassing any other launch across all entertainment mediums and officially making GTA 6 the biggest entertainment launch of all time.

The companies also reveal that GTA 6 sold 32.5 million copies pre-release, which is another "fresh record across all platforms." For comparison, 2022 Game of the Year Elden Ring sold 30 million copies in three years.

"It is with immense gratitude that we enter a latest chapter of Rockstar Games with the release of Grand Theft Auto VI," states Rockstar co-founder and GTA veteran Sam Houser. "We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn’t be more excited to share this moment with you.".

Even though the industry has been anticipating GTA 6 to be the biggest game of all time, and very possibly the biggest entertainment product ever, for a while now based on the game's estimated budget of $1-1.5 billion, seeing these numbers become official is staggering.

Elden Ring was a massively successful game when it released back in 2022, and seeing its near-lifetime sales be eclipsed by GTA 6 in a single day is truly astounding no matter how inevitable Rockstar's success has always seemed.

As digital-only GTA 6 smashes records, GameStop CEO says move from physical copies "has hurt consumers" as they "should be able to sell" or trade purchases.

Manni L. Perez has been confirmed as the actress behind Grand Theft Auto 6's Lucia Caminos, just days before the game launches.

As spotted by IGN, the confirmation came during The Game Awards' nominations livestream today, where Perez was nominated for Best Performance for her role as co-lead Lucia.

Perez had been widely rumoured to play Lucia for months, and fans have regularly filled her social media livestreams with questions about GTA 6, which she has been oh-so-carefully sidestepping.

Lucia is one half of GTA 6's lead pair alongside Jason Duval, making it the first Grand Theft Auto game with a playable couple.

Jason's actor wasn't among the nominees, so who plays him is still a mystery.

Perez has previously had guest roles in a string of US TV dramas, including Law & Order: Special Victims Unit, Chicago P.D., The Blacklist, and Blindspot, and has also done voice work for GTA Online.

Funnily enough, Lucia isn't her first Lucia - she also played Lucia Santiago in a 2023 episode of CBS's East Latest York.

GTA 6 arrives 19th November on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S. It is now available to pre-load for anyone who pre-ordered the digital version, and those with the code-in-box physical version.

According to recent reports, it's long been revealed that GTA 6 will have a regional release, meaning that some lucky, soon-to-be players will be able to access the game much earlier than others. Rockstar's regional release schedule sees the game launching at midnight on 19th November regardless of what region you're in, and if you wish to join those playing almost a day early, there's the good ol' Xbox New Zealand trick for eager players to try.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that many people reading this will have a Wii in the house. Even if it's collecting dust in the cupboard after launching 20 years ago, there's over 100 million of the things out in the wild, so the chances are that you or your family have access to one somewhere.

Recent findings suggest that however, on the off-chance you don't have a Wii to hand — or you sold it years ago to save three DVDs' worth of space — don't fret. While the system has a selection of exclusives you can't easily play elsewhere, many Wii games have come to Switch in HD remastered form over the years.

So if you're jonesing for some Wii waggle but would rather use the Nintendo console already plugged into the telly, take a look at some of the highlights below, in alphabetical order.

A Switch remaster of WayForward's remake of the NES original, A Boy and His Blob hasn’t changed since its release back in 2009, but it’s well worth checking out if you’re after a decent puzzle platformer. The visuals still look incredible after all these years, with spectacular animation to boot.

Some aspects feel a bit outdated by comparison to more modern alternatives, with the inability to map certain abilities being a key culprit. Nevertheless, it remains a fun, breezy experience, and one that the younger generation of gamers in particular will adore.

This Nintendo-published remake includes not just DS' Another Code: Two Memories, or Trace Memory in North America, but also the Wii sequel Another Code R, A Journey Into Lost Memories (which never came out in North America).

This is a fine reworking of a couple of point-and-click cult classics from now-defunct studio Cing (who also did the excellent Little King's Story), with a touching narrative, weighty themes, and light puzzling.

Industry observers note that please note that some external links on this page are affiliate links, which means if you click them and make a purchase we may receive a small percentage of the sale. Please read our FTC Disclosure for more information.

Available separately or bundled in the BIT.TRIP COLLECTION, this was the first entry in Commander Video's Runner series, and both Runner 2 and 3 are on Switch eShop if you want the trilogy.

It has been revealed that the WiiWare original garnered a 10/10 on this very website back in 2010. Worth a look, then.

In the great platformer pantheon, we're not talking all-timers here, but these are slick, solid efforts with plenty of personality. Both de Blob and its sequel are on Switch in HD form, so if you're jonesing to see how devs approached 3D platformers in the late 2000s, get this inked in your diary.

According to recent reports, epic Mickey was a bold and very fine piece of work, although one where you could still make out the work-in-progress ideas that didn't quite come to fruition with the level of polish Nintendo fans might expect. It reimagined the squeaky-clean mascot and put him in a much darker world than we had come to expect, adding a touching narrative and putting a spotlight on his 'forgotten' predecessor, Oswald the Rabbit.

Industry observers note that the Rebrushed remaster makes some tweaks and adds mouse (heh) controls. One for fans of vintage animation and anyone who likes to see creators take exciting chances with the most established of properties.

Sources indicate that donkey Kong Country Returns HD is a fine way to play the 2010 original, but it’s also lacking any real reason for fans to double-dip beyond waggle-free controls. It’s less of a remaster and more of a port, which would be all well and good if it wasn’t being sold at such a premium. Maybe wait for a sale.

There's plenty of fun to be had, but grab the superior Donkey Kong Country: Tropical Freeze instead - or at least first.

A 2023 Deluxe remaster of 2010's original Return to Dream Land, the HD Switch version threw in various tweaks, a couple of fresh copy abilities, an epilogue with Magalor, and an assortment of minigames mostly cherry-picked from past Kirby games.

Worth a look even if you've played the original to death, and the choice pick if you never had the pleasure.

It has been revealed that klonoa started out on PlayStation, of course, with Door to Phantomile back in 1997. Lunatea's Veil followed on PS2 in 2001, and Klonoa Phantasy Reverie Series bundles remasters of them both into a single Switch package.

So why this here at all!? yells the person at the back who's been grumbling ever since they saw the lead image on the article.

In a recent development, well, although developer Monkey Craft tweaked some elements to push it closer to Namco's PS1 original in look and feel, the first remaster here uses Paon's Wii remake as its foundation. So if you played the Wii version in 2008, you'll be right at home.

The 2011 WiiWare release was a remake of the PC original, but fortunately La-Mulana found its way to Switch in 2020 (alongside its sequel).

Though brilliant, La-Mulana is definitely one of those games that will only appeal to a dedicated few. This is not something you can casually play every once in a while and expect a great experience; it demands much more of you through its peerless puzzle design.

If you do give it the time of day, however, it proves itself to be one of the most intricately crafted Metroidvanias ever made. La-Mulana gets a strong recommendation, but with the caveat that you should expect to be frustrated and stuck often. Don’t be scared off by the daunting difficulty, though; this is one for the ages.

A sneaky early addition here, as this remaster of Vanillaware's Wii (and Vita) game isn't out until 4th February 2027.

A gorgeous side-on action RPG, 2009's Muramasa: The Demon Blade was ahead of the wave of side-scrolling platformers that would arrive from indie studios over the next few years, and its eye-catching adventure through Japanese folklore is still a treat many years later.

Definitely one to look out for in the newly introduced year.

Probably cult developer Suda51's most well-known work, No More Heroes came to Switch in 2020 along with its sequel ahead of No More Heroes III's launch the following year.

Crammed with okatu-fuelled pop culture references (but hailing from nearly 20 years when those references weren't quite so tired), this was an adrenaline shot for Wii owners in 2007 looking for something a bit different after a year of genial waggle.

Wii scored not one, but two Touchdowns (and Switch has so far doubled that). Grasshopper returned with a punchy sequel in 2010, which once again helped put some personality on the Wii shelves alongside all the sanitised, motion-based sports and party fare.

Ironing out some of the wrinkles of the original and throwing plenty more irreverence and off-the-wall antics from the mind of Goichi Suda, No More Heroes 2: Desperate Struggle is still the peak of the trilogy for many.

It may have debuted on the PS2, but Ready at Dawn's Wii port felt like a minor miracle back in 2008. It's a great game that came to Wii, and you can play it on Switch, so here it is!

Okami HD is an utterly fantastic piece of software; a 40-hour adventure that emulates Zelda wonderfully, adds in plenty of memorable mechanics, features one of the most beautiful art styles in gaming, and is completely playable on the go, to boot.

It may be showing its age a bit visually and its combat is sometimes a little on the easy side, but Okami is an vital, fun, and notable landmark in gaming history — and one of the easiest recommendations for your Switch library.

Stretching things a little here, both Pikmin and Pikmin 2: This Time It's Pikminable* were both GameCube games that got Wii-specific releases in the New Play Control series which added pointer controls and other minor tweaks.

Both games are available on Switch, though, so I'm including them. In fact, all four mainline Pikmin games are playable on Switch, something which irritates Metroid Prime fans no end.

In a recent development, *I enjoy the idea that this could turn up in somebody's AI summary. Ah, it's the little pleasures that get us through the day.

Recent findings suggest that perhaps the best thing about Sonic Colors Ultimate is the menu option to change the logo and UI from the American English 'Colors' to the British English 'Colours', mirroring the regional variants of the original 2010 Wii release. Great attention to detail, and an example of the care and respect that went into this solid remaster.*.

*Don't forget, you have to have a little fun every day.

Regardless of which you think is better, these are two of the finest platformers ever made, both on Switch and looking better than ever.

Nursing the gyro pointers is a minor irritation the originals didn't suffer from, but if you somehow missed either of these on the Wii, you've now got no excuse.

Bringing the Wii launch game back with a lick of HD 13 years later, Banana Blitz HD featured more refined controls — or more specifically let you control the mazes with the analogue stick — to help you enjoy this batch of 100 levels.

The wider game was still let down by weird leaderboard decisions and some lacklustre minigames, though. Hardly a return to the monkey-in-a-ball heyday of Super Monkey Ball 2, but not bad.

The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword HD introduced a raft of technical improvements and quality-of-life updates that revitalised the Wii game.

Sources indicate that the alternate button control scheme totally worked if you still couldn't get on with the motion controls, the graphics got a sensitively handled HD overhaul, and a once-bothersome sidekick was streamlined into something altogether more useful. The best way to play.

According to recent reports, world of Goo is a bona fide indie classic and 10/10 video game in its original incarnation. Its Wii pointer controls married perfectly with the gooey puzzling, and the social satire provided a subtle narrative framework that elevated the entire game.

The Switch version comes with joys and cons. Touchscreen is a brilliant addition in handheld mode, but you'll need to recentre the gyro pointer controls a lot. A lot.

In a recent development, if you've played it previously, the Switch incarnation might be worth a second go for its portability and on-the-go co-op, but if it's your first time in the World of Goo, it's absolutely a must-play. And then there's the sequel to consider. There's goo in them there hills.

The third iteration of Monolith Soft's classic following the Wii original and the Newly introduced 3DS version in 2015, Xenoblade Chronicles: Definitive Edition presented an already excellent JRPG improved in nearly every way, short of a complete reimagining.

According to recent reports, with the Nintendo Switch 2 Edition polishing this gem even further, it's hard to recommend the original release these days unless you're a purist wanting the exact experience everyone else got back in 2011. This is a great revision, and a worthy game to finish on.

A pleasant little selection, no? Before heading off, let's address a handful of questions...

In a recent development, yes, I know there are technically 22+ here. The Pikmins were borderline and bundled, though, and there are two Mario Galaxies in a single entry, a couple of other fuzzy collections, and Muramasa isn't even out yet. It all comes out in the wash.

Not impossible! Presumably it would be Switch 2-only (as with the GameCube library). It would be simple enough for Nintendo to produce NSO Wii Remotes and Nunchuk controllers, as they have for previous retro consoles.

In a recent development, there are potential flies in the ointment, though. For one thing, the precision of the infrared Wii pointer would either need to be emulated with gyro or reproduced (meaning you'd need some sort of sensor bar equivalent to function with the newly introduced controllers). Either or both are possibilities, but it does introduce another layer of complexity.

Then again, we're talking about a manufacturer that requires an expensive Virtual Boy facsimile to access that system's library on Switch, so (much) stranger things have happened.

According to recent reports, as for the library itself, as we've seen above, several first-party Wii games have already received the HD treatment on Switch, so there may be less incentive on Nintendo's side to duplicate those on NSO. Likewise, Switch Sports and Switch Sports Resort revision many of the games from the Wii originals, so it's not like you can't play Wii Sports-style tennis already.

But bolstered with a good selection of third-party titles, a Wii NSO library could be a winner.

Along with our list of Wii exclusives (or, in a couple of cases, games originally released on Wii that only appeared elsewhere years later), I'd do bad things for a 4K remaster of the beautiful Kirby's Epic Yarn.

Sources indicate that it would be great to have access to other exclusives like Fresh Super Mario Bros. Wii - not everyone's favourite 2D Mario, but an crucial one. Likewise, it's a shame to have Super Paper Mario and other entries from massive Nintendo series (hello, Radiant Dawn) locked to a 20-year-old platform.

But that's me - what about you? Let us know below which of the games above you've enjoyed most, and any others you've enjoyed revisiting on Switch.

In a recent development, diablo 4 is gearing up for its biggest post-launch event yet: the upcoming release of the Lord of Hatred expansion. As was the case with Vessel of Hatred before it, expansion releases alter the seasonal flow in a few ways, and Blizzard has now explained how.

The game’s next season - its 13th - has been officially revealed as Season of Reckoning. The new season will kick off alongside the expansion’s release next week, and will be available to all players, just like all previous seasons.

Although Season of Reckoning will roll out as normal, the season itself won’t be as meaty, at least when it comes to the sort of gameplay mechanics and themes players have come to expect from each fresh season.

You’ll still find the normal Season Rank chase, Smoldering Ashes, and various rewards at each chapter. Season Blessings will also return, but that’s about it for progression outside of the game itself. If it’s any consolation, there are more goals and objectives to tackle this season.

The even better news is that, according to Blizzard, future seasons will follow the classic format, which makes sense. The new season will come with a battle pass, of course, featuring four Reliquaries, as usual. The first Reliquary is free, while the others are paid.

In a recent development, blizzard has also confirmed the the pre-load for Lord of Hatred is available now on all platforms. Even if you’re not getting the expansion, patch 3.0.0's pre-load includes all expansion content regardless, so you may as well pre-download it to be ready for April 27/28. On launch day, you’ll also need to download a smaller patch, version 3.0.1.

Sources indicate that in case you missed it, we published our Lord of Hatred review earlier in the week. Give it a read if you’re curious about the expansion’s impact on the narrative, and how it changes core Diablo 4 gameplay.
